target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove major scheduling barriers and increase access to voting for low-income workers.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many low-income workers are in retail and service jobs that still work holidays, so the holiday would not reliably free the workers most constrained by schedules.

target: AG1's underlying assumption that a holiday-only policy would significantly increase turnout by easing scheduling barriers.
objection: Research shows that an election holiday, by itself, is not an effective way to raise voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's claim that school scheduling is a major reason a national holiday would improve access to voting.
objection: Federal holiday status does not automatically change school calendars; school closures are decided by state and local districts, and many districts would likely keep normal sessions even on a federal holiday.

target: AG2's objection that a holiday would not help because some low-income workers would still have to work.
objection: Even if some retail or service workers still work on Election Day, the holiday can still reduce barriers for many other voters by easing school-related scheduling constraints, so the criticism does not defeat the broader access benefit.

target: AG2's claim that schools would probably keep operating normally despite a national holiday.
objection: A national holiday would be observed by schools and change day-to-day school operations, and there is no evidence that most schools would continue normal sessions despite the holiday designation.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday does not only solve time-off barriers and therefore lacks broader civic value.
objection: Making voting a holiday also frames it as a civic celebration, which can strengthen civic motivation and increase participation beyond merely giving people more time off.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers are the main concern and that a holiday is too narrow to matter broadly.
objection: Work scheduling constraints affect a broad range of voters, not just workers in one narrow category, so the holiday addresses a wider set of barriers than AG2 suggests.

target: AG2's assumption that a holiday must fully eliminate every work conflict to be worthwhile.
objection: National holidays generally change workplace scheduling, with many employers closing or reducing operations, so a federal Election Day holiday would reduce work pressure for many employees even if some essential workers still have to work.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday remains justified because it need not eliminate every barrier for every person.
objection: If the policy does not substantially help the most constrained voters, then it fails the core access purpose AG1 relies on; partial benefit is not enough if the main barrier remains for those most affected.

target: AG1's use of international precedent to support the practicality of an Election Day holiday.
objection: Even if other democracies hold elections on weekends or holidays, that does not show a U.S. federal holiday would work, because U.S. private employers are not required to give time off or paid time to vote.

target: AG2's objection that the holiday would not reliably free low-income workers because private employers need not close or pay them.
objection: In practice, a national holiday changes the day's status and typically leads workplaces to adjust staffing and schedules, so it would substantially reduce work-versus-voting pressure for many workers even without a legal paid-time-off mandate.

target: AG2's claim that OECD weekend/holiday election practices do not support a U.S. holiday because the U.S. would lack a non-workday mechanism.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does align the election with the kind of non-standard scheduling used in comparable democracies, so the absence of a separate paid-time-off rule does not show the holiday is inherently unworkable.

target: AG1's reliance on OECD weekend/holiday election precedent to argue that a U.S. holiday would work for voters.
objection: OECD weekend elections often occur on days people are already off work under the normal weekly schedule, so that precedent does not prove a U.S. weekday converted into a federal holiday would reliably become a non-work day for work-constrained voters.

target: AG1's claim that OECD precedent undermines the concern about low-income workers being disadvantaged.
objection: If OECD weekend/holiday evidence does not show that a U.S. weekday holiday would reliably give work-constrained voters time off, then it does not rebut the concern that low-income workers would still be disadvantaged by the holiday approach.
